Right: the 2-crust keeps every node with coreness 2 or less, so E, F, G, H and the edges among them are in the accent color, and only the 3-core A to D is dashed." width="100%"} The k-crust contains all nodes with coreness <= `k`. This is the complement of nodes with high coreness values. Put differently, the k-crust is what remains after deleting the `(k+1)`-core: the union of the shells `0` through `k`, i.e., the network's periphery. It is the counterpart of `k_core()`, and is useful for: - studying the periphery of a network separately from its dense core - checking how the outer layers are organized once the core is removed (for example, whether they fall apart into many small pieces) - removing a dominant core before looking for smaller communities The returned graph contains only the crust's nodes and the edges between them; edges into the removed core are dropped. To get every node's coreness at once, use `coreness()`; see also `k_shell()` for a single layer. Degrees count edges without weights. For directed graphs, degree means out-degree. The original graph is not modified. The returned graph keeps the node and edge IDs, labels, weights and attributes of the original. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Maximum coreness value to include. Must be a non-negative integer. `k=0` keeps only isolated nodes, and any `k` at or above the graph's maximum coreness keeps the whole graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New graph containing only the k-crust nodes and their connecting edges. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The graph below has a dense cluster (A, B, C, D, coreness 3), a loop E-F-G attached to it (coreness 2), and a pendant node H (coreness 1). The 2-crust removes the cluster and keeps the outer layers, the loop plus H: ::: {#9a6c781a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("C", "E"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "G"), ("G", "D"), ("G", "H")]) ) crust_2 = graph.k_crust(2) sorted(crust_2.get_node_df()["label"].to_list()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['E', 'F', 'G', 'H'] ``` ::: ::: Only the edges among those four nodes survive (E-F, F-G, and G-H), so the crust is a simple chain: ::: {#dcbcd8a2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} (crust_2.count_nodes(), crust_2.count_edges()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (4, 3) ``` ::: ::: Raising `k` to the maximum coreness (here `3`) gives back every node and edge: ::: {#f9395b07 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} crust_3 = graph.k_crust(3) (crust_3.count_nodes(), crust_3.count_edges()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (8, 12) ``` ::: :::
